item1.title: Dental Bridges
item1.value: Dental bridges are literally a bridge to fill the gap of your missing teeth. They close the gap of a single missing tooth or multiple missing teeth.
item1.value2: The two natural teeth in front and behind the gap are used as bridge pillars. That is, if one tooth gap is to be filled, two of your teeth are cut and reduced to be used as pillars.
item1.value3: This is the basic idea, but bridges can vary depending on how many teeth are missing, where they are located in the mouth, and the type of bridge used.
item1.value4: Bridges, like any dental prosthesis, have pros and cons, risks, and benefits.

item2.title: Types of Dental Bridges
item2.value: If you have missing teeth in your mouth, your dentist may mention several types of dental bridges. It may be better for you to be a little familiar with this topic in advance.
item2.value3: It is called 'traditional' because it is the most commonly used and best-known type. It is the most common method for completing one or more missing teeth. The teeth on both sides of the missing tooth are cut and reduced to make prosthetic teeth in the form of a bridge.
item2.value4: Traditional bridges can be used anywhere in the mouth as long as you have natural teeth on both sides of the missing tooth or teeth.
item2.value5: The biggest disadvantage is that the enamel of the tooth must be completely cut and reduced before placing your prosthesis. It should be remembered that since enamel does not grow back, these teeth will always be vulnerable and prone to decay.
item2.value7: A prosthetic bridge consisting of a metal or porcelain frame with teeth in front, usually attached to adjacent natural teeth with one or two wings.
item2.value8: Using a Maryland Bridge has many benefits. It is a conservative, low-risk replacement option that is very strong (thanks to the composite resin it is made of and its adhesion to your natural teeth). They can also look very realistic and can be a permanent option.
item2.value9: However, it can be difficult to perfectly match the fake tooth to the space left by the missing tooth. Therefore, your dentist may need to cut your surrounding teeth during placement to ensure the pontic(s) fit properly. Furthermore, this is the most expensive type of dental bridge.
item2.value10: Although adhesive dentistry has seen many developments in recent years, Maryland bridges have fallen out of favor for some time due to concerns about aspirating the prosthesis if it becomes loose due to chewing forces. This type of bridge is usually indicated only for replacing front teeth, but can be successful in the posterior region in certain cases.
item2.value12: If you have only one natural tooth that can be used as an abutment, you can get a cantilever bridge.
item2.value13: They are very similar to traditional bridges, the main difference being that they have only one supporting tooth instead of a tooth on each side of the mouth.
item2.value14: It has similar pros and cons to traditional bridges, such as removing enamel. However, because there is only one supporting tooth, this can lead to problems such as a broken tooth or loosening of the crown.
item2.value16: Whether you are missing multiple teeth in a row or across your mouth, you may consider implant-supported bridges.
item2.value17: Although ideal when there are several missing teeth next to each other, it is also an excellent option for those missing teeth that are not close to each other.
item2.value18: As the name suggests, these bridges are secured with dental implants. Typically, you get one implant for each missing tooth, and the bridge attaches to these implants. If this is not possible, your dentist can secure all prostheses with just two implant-supported crowns. This would be a much more affordable option.
item2.value19: There are four main types of dental bridges, each serving a different purpose: Cantilever, Implant-Supported, Maryland, and Traditional.

item3.title: How is the Dental Bridge Procedure?
item3.value: After consulting your dentist and deciding on a dental bridge, you will schedule your first visit for the procedure.
item3.value2: During this first visit, the dentist will prepare the abutment teeth. This involves removing some enamel from adjacent teeth to allow crowns to be placed over them.
item3.value3: The dentist will then take an impression of your teeth to create the bridge, fake tooth, and crown using the best available material (usually porcelain, ceramic, and/or metal). Since the bridge will likely be made by a dental laboratory, you may not get the new one that day. Thus, your dentist will create a removable dental bridge for you to wear temporarily. It helps protect exposed teeth and still allows teeth in between.
item3.value4: During the second visit, your dentist will remove the temporary bridge and place the new, permanent dental bridge. It can be made of porcelain, metal, or both. They will check to ensure a proper fit and adjust as necessary.
item3.value5: You may need to make multiple visits for your dentist to continue checking fit and adjusting to ensure it stays secure and comfortable.
item3.value6: The dental bridge placement procedure is as follows: treatment of the area, removal of the temporary bridge, placement of the permanent dental bridge, and follow-up visits.

item4.title: Dental Bridge Cost
item4.value: What is the cost of a dental bridge? How much will the insurance company cover? Will Medicaid pay for your dental bridge?
item4.value2: The answers to these questions depend on various factors, but the average cost of a dental bridge can range from $500 to $1,200 per unit (including abutments and pontics).
item4.value3: But here are a few of these determining factors:
item4.value5: • Whether the bridge was made in a dental laboratory or in the dentist's office
item4.value7: • The knowledge, experience, and location of the dentist
item4.value8: • Your insurance plan or Medicaid coverage
item4.value9: To get a more accurate estimate of the cost of your dental bridge, it is best to talk to your dentist and insurance company to see what is covered.
item4.value10: The cost of a dental bridge can be $1,200 or more (depending on insurance and decision factors).

item5.title: Common Problems
item5.value: My Dental Bridge Hurts
item5.value2: Call your dentist and make an appointment. They can understand why it hurts and how to fix it. In the meantime, you can get a denture pain cream to help soothe discomfort.
item5.value4: If you experience any of the following symptoms, you may have a loose dental bridge:
item5.value6: • Your teeth and/or gums are very sensitive
item5.value9: • A bad taste in your mouth (from food stuck between the bridge or related tooth decay)
item5.value10: If you have a loose bridge, the best option is to visit your dentist's office as soon as possible. However, sometimes this is not immediately possible, and you might want a solution in the meantime. Here is how you can fix a loose dental bridge at home if comfortable making adjustments yourself:
item5.value11: 1. Buy dental cement from your local pharmacy
item5.value12: 2. Clean the inside of the bridge
item5.value14: 4. Follow the instructions that come with the dental cement (instructions vary, so this step is important)
item5.value15: 5. Clean off excess cement after it hardens
item5.value17: If your dental bridge comes out and falls, you first want to talk to your dentist. They may want to see you in person. In the meantime, you can try these steps to put your replacement back in place:
item5.value19: 2. Place the crown over the desired tooth to test fit
item5.value20: 3. With little or no pressure, close your teeth together to ensure the crown is correctly aligned
item5.value21: 4. Then remove the crown and fill part of it with denture adhesive
item5.value22: 5. Place the crown back onto the tooth
item5.value23: 6. Again, with little or no pressure, close your teeth to ensure it works correctly

item6.title: Conclusion
item6.value: Now you know the four main types of dental bridges. Just as a refresher: Cantilever, Implant-Supported, Maryland, and Traditional. Each serves a different purpose, so you and your dentist choose the most suitable option.
item6.value2: Hopefully, this guide has helped you know how to prepare mentally for the procedure. Knowing the steps and length of this process will help you prepare. In summary, your dentist will first treat the area, then remove the temporary bridge, place the permanent dental bridge, and schedule follow-up visits.

item1.title: How Long Does a Dental Bridge Last?
item1.value: It depends on the type of bridge, the quality of the procedure, how your body reacts to and adapts to the replacements. However, generally speaking, a dental bridge can last between five and fifteen years.

item2.title: Is Getting a Dental Bridge Painful?
item2.value: The short answer is yes, it can be in some cases. Obviously, your dentist will use anesthesia, but you may experience some tooth and jaw pain after the procedure and in the following weeks. However, it is very common for patients to be perfectly comfortable after the procedure. Everyone's teeth react differently.

item3.title: How Is a Dental Bridge Repaired?
item3.value: The simple answer: take it to your dentist for repair. Trying to repair it yourself is probably not a good idea.

item4.title: How long does it take to get a dental bridge?
item4.value: Usually only a few days (see “How is the Dental Bridge Procedure?” above).

item5.title: How Is a Dental Bridge Made?
item5.value: Typically, a bridge is made by a dental laboratory using porcelain with a metal framework or acrylic. Although sometimes the dentist's office may fabricate a bridge in-house.

item6.title: How Should I Clean My Dental Bridge?
item6.value: Basically, you should clean and maintain your dental bridges like your natural teeth. This includes brushing and flossing. However, because it is a prosthesis, you will want to get under the fake tooth with a denture brush or oral irrigator.

item1.title: What is bad breath (Halitosis)?
item1.value: Unpleasant and disturbing odor in the mouth is briefly called bad breath or 'halitosis'. Bad breath cannot be defined as a disease by itself, but it can be a precursor to important diseases. Pathological bad breath originating from disease is in this class, and there is also physiological bad breath that can occur even in healthy individuals. Bad breath caused by the food we eat or when we wake up in the morning is physiological bad breath and is not a sign of disease.
item1.value2: Bad breath (halitosis) negatively affects the person's communication with people around them and also causes social pressure and self-confidence issues. Patients usually consult dentists for bad breath upon warning from people around them. After tooth decay and periodontal diseases, bad breath is the most common reason for patients to visit dentists. Although halitosis is seen in almost half of the population, very few patients come to the dentist for treatment.
item1.value3: If there is no oral cause explaining bad breath, blockage of the nasal passages or pharyngeal obstructions called adenoids lead to mouth breathing. Since mouth breathing causes oral dryness, it not only causes halitosis but should also be kept in mind that it causes tooth decay because teeth cannot be cleaned properly.

item2.title: Who gets bad breath?
item2.value: Bad breath is more common in middle-aged adults and men. Also, dental prostheses used in advanced age, decreased saliva flow, and systemic diseases cause halitosis.

item3.title: What are the causes of bad breath?
item3.value: • Bad breath after eating or upon waking up is defined as physiological bad breath and is not a sign of disease. Bad breath occurring otherwise is usually considered a sign of disease and is defined as pathological bad breath.
item3.value2: • Plaque and food residues between teeth; brushing alone is not enough, dental floss must be used. Using dental floss in addition to brushing greatly contributes to solving this problem.
item3.value3: • Smoking; besides its own bad odor, dental and gum diseases it causes are reasons for halitosis. The smell of smoke itself lasts 24 hours. Also, excessive smoking causes furring and hairiness on the tongue, which leads to food and plaque accumulation (called 'tongue coating'),
item3.value4: • Tongue coating; when the tongue surface is covered with a brownish coating, bacteria that form sulfur compounds also cause bad breath. Brushing the tongue is very important to eliminate tongue coating.
item3.value5: • Dental plaque, tartar, gum diseases; These problems can be easily eliminated by dentists. Scaling at least once a year is very important for gum health.
item3.value6: • Stomach problems such as reflux, gastritis, ulcers; digestive system (gastrointestinal system) disorders are one of the most common causes of bad breath. The frequency of occurrence increases especially in spring, known as season transitions. Patients usually consult dentists with a complaint of bad breath, but it is often confused with breath odor rather than bad breath. For these problems, it is recommended to consult a general surgeon and undergo endoscopy.
item3.value7: • Upper Respiratory Tract Infections, pharyngitis, sinusitis; such disorders are also very common causes of bad breath because they cause post-nasal drip. It is best to distinguish this properly and refer to an ENT specialist.

item1.title: Why Are There So Many Dental Implants? And What Is This 'All-On-4'?
item1.value: To understand what an All-On-4 dental implant is, you first need to know what an implant is. A dental implant is basically a small (titanium) screw placed into your jawbone in the space left by a missing tooth. After the implant is placed in your mouth, your dentist will add a prosthetic tooth to the dental implant. Now, multiply that idea by four and you get an All-On-4 dental implant. Instead of using one implant for each missing tooth, you can use four main screws: four implants on top and four on the bottom. Then your dentist can attach dentures to these implants. It should be well known that four implants may not always be the best option, so it is more beneficial to always consult your doctor for the most accurate result.

item2.title: What is the Cost of a Four-Unit Dental Implant?
item2.value: The cost of All-On-4 dental implants can vary depending on the material used and how many prosthetic teeth you need.

item3.title: Acrylic or Composite All-On-4 Dental Prostheses
item3.value: This is the standard All-On-4 option. It involves using an acrylic prosthesis built on top of 4 titanium implants. This type of prosthesis is more often used in the first 3 to 6 months. It has a lower cost. It is essentially suitable for continuous use as well, but many patients rightly replace them with porcelain teeth after the first stage for superior aesthetic appearance.

item4.title: Porcelain All-On-4 Dental Prostheses
item4.value: Prostheses made of porcelain look more aesthetic and realistic. They also last longer than acrylic, but this type of porcelain prosthesis is an additional cost. Thus, the entire procedure and prosthesis may result in a higher cost.

MainContent.title: How is the All-On-4 Dental Implant Procedure?
MainContent.item1: Getting a dental implant for the first time can be scary. The idea of getting 4 at once might also make you nervous. Much of this fear probably stems from uncertainty, so let's take a look at the step-by-step process of getting an All-On-4 dental implant.
MainContent.item2: First; your dentist will want to make you comfortable, so local or general anesthesia will be administered. This is entirely a decision you and your dentist will make together. If your dentist and anesthesiologist find it appropriate, general anesthesia can sometimes be the most comfortable option. But it should be known that a very large proportion of such procedures can be easily handled with local anesthesia.
MainContent.item3: Second; your dentist will prepare your mouth for implants by removing any remaining unhealthy teeth, diseased or infected tissue from your jaw and gums.
MainContent.item4: Then; they will begin the implant placement process. This means they will place titanium screws into your jawbone. Most likely, two implants will be placed towards the front of your mouth and two towards the back, so that the 'titanium screws' can evenly bear the force of the denture.
MainContent.item5: After the implants are placed, your dentist will thoroughly clean the wound areas and suture all incised areas. Then you will be taken to a recovery room where you can rest.
MainContent.item6: The basic All-On-4 implant procedure includes anesthesia, preparation of the surgical site, implant placement, and post-operative cleaning and suturing.

MainContent.title: Healing Time of All-On-4 Dental Implants
MainContent.value: After traditional prostheses are placed, the healing time can vary from 3 to 8 months, but after an All-On-4 prosthesis is placed, permanent porcelains can be placed earlier. The reason is that the implants integrate with your bone and increase prosthesis stability from day one.

item1.title: The First Day
item1.item1: During the first hour after your surgery, or until bleeding stops, you need to gently bite on the gauze pads placed over the surgical areas. After the first hour, you may be asked to remove the gauze unless there is excessive bleeding, in which case your dentist will likely replace it with new gauze.
item1.item2: When you return home from surgery, make sure you don't do anything that could harm the surgical areas. Do not rinse or touch the surgical areas except for gentle brushing with a soft toothbrush. Obviously, smoking later (and generally) greatly affects the healing of surgical areas. It is also important to keep your mouth as clean as possible. Your doctor will likely prescribe medication to prevent bacterial infection and promote healing.
item1.item3: Twenty-four hours after surgery, if there is a small amount of bleeding, you can gently rinse your mouth with salt water. Just mix one tablespoon of salt with a glass of water and rinse slowly. You can do this 2-3 times a day.

item2.title: Days After Surgery
item2.item1: The best thing you can do in the time following surgery is to rest. Among the things you should not do are bending, lifting heavy objects, or engaging in strenuous activities that could lead to more bleeding and swelling.
item2.item2: Also, it is best to get up slowly and carefully from a lying position. Otherwise, you might feel dizzy. If you are a person who normally exercises, you should avoid it for 3-4 days after surgery.
item2.item3: The most important things to remember during recovery are rest, no smoking or alcohol consumption, pain management, and eating soft foods.

MainContent.title: Some Common Problems That May Occur After Surgery
MainContent.value: Some general problems you may encounter in the days following surgery and how to care for your All-On-4 dental implants are explained below.

item1.title: Persistent Bleeding
item1.value: If you notice that bleeding does not stop, this is usually because you are not biting on the gauze pads directly over the surgical areas. Reposition the gauze and check if bleeding has stopped. If this doesn't work and bleeding continues, try sitting upright, avoid physical activity, and apply ice packs to the outside of your mouth. Then biting on a moist black tea bag for about 30 minutes will also help you. If this still doesn't help, be sure to call your dentist to make an appointment.

item2.title: Swelling
item2.value: Swelling is a normal part of having surgery and peaks about 2-3 days after the procedure. Using ice or a cold pack over your cheek within the first 24 hours following the procedure can help keep swelling to a minimum (apply cold for 10 minutes and rest for 10 minutes). Applying cold continuously without a break can cause cold burns (even if you don't feel it initially due to numbness). Also, your dentist may prescribe medication to minimize swelling.

item3.title: Pain
item3.value: This is an inevitable outcome of this surgery. Your dentist will give you painkillers, and you must take them as directed. It should be remembered that smoking and eating/drinking hot foods certainly increase pain and swelling. If you think you need more medication to control pain, call your dentist.

item4.title: Restricted Diet
item4.value: As long as the foods you eat do not cause discomfort, there is no harm in eating. You should avoid hard foods, candies, or very hot foods, and chewing is not recommended until the numbness in your tongue and lips subsides. Our best advice is to consume only liquid or pureed foods for the first few days after surgery. Most importantly, make sure you are well nourished, no matter how uncomfortable it may be. It is very important for your healing.

item5.title: Nausea
item5.value: You may experience nausea or even vomiting due to accidentally swallowed blood or the medications you will take. If nausea persists or worsens, call your dentist for advice.

item6.title: Bruising
item6.value: About 2-3 days after surgery, you may see discoloration or bruising near the surgical areas. This is a natural result of the surgery and is quite normal. Applying mild heat to your cheek after the first 48 hours following the procedure will help bruising to disperse more quickly.

item7.title: Sharp Protrusions in Your Mouth
item7.value: If you start to feel sharp protrusions like splinters in your mouth, especially in the areas where your teeth were extracted, these may be bone walls of the extracted teeth. After a few days, small bone fragments of extracted teeth may protrude slightly from the gums and cause discomfort. You should not worry about this; you can discuss this with your dentist.

item8.title: Dry Lips
item8.value: Since your mouth will be open for a long time and your lips will stretch slightly while biting the gauze, it is expected that your lips may be dry or the corners of your lips may be irritated. Small tears or cold sores may occur on the corners of the lips. You can use Vaseline or another moisturizing ointment.

item9.title: Sore Throat
item9.value: Because your mouth may be open most of the time due to the gauze, this can lead to a sore throat and make swallowing painful. This is a temporary symptom that usually disappears after a few days.

item10.title: Stiff Muscles
item10.value: Your jaw muscles may contract from opening your jaw for a long time and holding it in the same position. For this, you can slowly stretch your jaw from time to time, and if your dentist deems it appropriate, they may give muscle relaxants. If you experience any of these symptoms or problems, the first thing you should do is contact your dentist, even if you think everything is fine.

item11.title: Common Problems with 4-Unit Dental Implants
item11.value: Sometimes you may encounter problems after the healing process. The most common problems you may encounter with All-On-4 implants are:

item12.title: Surgical Complications
item12.value: With any type of surgery, there are always associated risks. Possible complications with the All-On-4 procedure in particular include infection, poor healing, and excessive bleeding. Obviously, your dentist will do everything possible to avoid these risks, but sometimes they happen. After surgery, it is best to watch for these complications and report any abnormal changes to your dentist.

item13.title: Dental Implants That Do Not Integrate with Your Bone
item13.value: Sometimes dental implants and your bone do not agree. Factors that determine how well an implant will integrate into your bone include smoking, the quality of your bone density, your nutrition, and many other things. If an implant does not integrate with your bone, your dentist may remove the implant, allow the area to heal, and place a new implant.

item14.title: Failed Implants
item14.value: This is a rare occurrence, but it is still a possibility. Dental implants have an extremely high success rate; however, if they fail, your dentist may either replace the implant immediately with a new one or allow the area to heal and re-implant after a few months. The most common cause of failed implants is gum problems, which you can prevent by taking good care of your gums and going for regular check-ups.

MainContent.title: What Are Your Temporary Tooth Options While Waiting for Implant Healing?
MainContent.value: For many patients, the process of deciding on and getting a dental implant is known to be confusing and difficult. Then, the process of making your permanent dental prostheses will begin. This is a relatively less confusing and more enjoyable process since you are at the end. However, there is also your temporary teeth during the healing period and their options, which are forgotten or overlooked. In this article, we will discuss exactly that: your temporary dental prostheses and options during the healing period after getting an implant. You should know that if you and your dentist decide that a temporary tooth is needed during this process (generally, a temporary prosthesis is not required for aesthetic reasons in the back areas and may not be preferred), you have many options.

item1.title: Temporary Single Tooth Crown
item1.value: When it comes to temporary teeth, although not always possible, a cemented temporary crown is the best. But it can cause problems, so it is not ideal or suitable for every patient. What is done here is cementing the crown (the tooth-looking part of the implant) to the implant's abutment.

positiveOps.title: Pros
positiveOps.item1: Quickly fills the missing tooth space.
positiveOps.item2: Since it is cemented, it does not need to be removed for cleaning.
positiveOps.item4: The surrounding gum tissue forms properly around the temporary tooth. This benefits the aesthetics of the future permanent tooth.
positiveOps.item5: When making the permanent tooth later, impressions can be taken directly without having to cut open the implant again.

negativeOps.title: Cons
negativeOps.item1: Too much pressure on the tooth can break the implant.
negativeOps.item2: The initial procedure is longer and more expensive.
negativeOps.item3: You may plan to get a temporary tooth, but it may not be possible on the same day as the procedure.

item2.title: Temporary Denture
item2.value: About 7-10 days after your implants are placed, your dentist will want to see you again for both suture removal and a check-up. If everything is going well and your wounds are healing very properly, a temporary denture can be made. But dentists may not always want this. These dentures can cause disproportionate and undetermined pressure on the underlying dental implants. Disproportionate forces can sometimes adversely affect the healing process of the implant.

positiveOps.title: Pros
positiveOps.item1: Affordable (probably the cheapest artificial tooth option).
positiveOps.item2: Made quickly within 1-2 days, in-office or at a laboratory.
positiveOps.item3: High success rate in appropriate cases.
positiveOps.item4: If done carefully, does not put excessive pressure on your dental implant.
positiveOps.item5: The fastest, cheapest, and easiest solution for most cases.

negativeOps.title: Cons
negativeOps.item1: A removable denture rarely perfectly fits your natural teeth.
negativeOps.item2: If you have had bone grafting or gum surgery, it can put unnecessary pressure on the gums. This can negatively affect the healing process.
negativeOps.item3: Can easily break or fall out of your mouth.
negativeOps.item4: Eating may be difficult because they are not strong enough.
negativeOps.item5: Food can get underneath as they are removable.
negativeOps.item7: Uncomfortable, can be bulky and irritating.

item3.title: Temporary Dental Bridges
item3.value: They are usually made of acrylic material. A temporary dental bridge can be a more durable option compared to others. It relies on surrounding teeth for support. However, temporary dental bridges can lead to long-term sensitivity and even decay of healthy teeth.

item4.title: Essix Plates
item4.value: Essix plates are transparent plates that sit on all of your lower or upper teeth. You may be familiar with these plates because they are often given to patients for night teeth grinding.

positiveOps.title: Pros
positiveOps.item1: Essix plates are one of the most comfortable options for a removable prosthesis.
positiveOps.item2: Quick and easy to make (usually within 1-2 days).
positiveOps.item4: Does not put pressure on areas where you have had gum surgery or bone grafting.

negativeOps.title: Cons
negativeOps.item1: It is difficult to get a perfect match, so it may not fit perfectly.
negativeOps.item2: Because it is removable, food can get underneath, and it must be cleaned after every meal.
negativeOps.item3: Difficulty and difference in speech may occur.
negativeOps.item4: Can be lost if you are not careful.

Finally.title: In Summary
Finally.value: Not all dental implants are permanent and fixed. As you can see in this article, you have many options for temporary dental implant teeth.
Finally.value2: You have many options, and choosing one yourself is both difficult and may not be exactly correct. Therefore, you and your dentist should decide together.
Finally.value3: Ask your dentist everything about your treatment and do not hesitate to ask again and again if you are not sure you understand your treatment options correctly.

Always seek the advice of your doctor, dentist, or other qualified health provider with any questions you may have regarding a medical condition.

Burksizm.title: Why Do We Grind Our Teeth at Night or During the Day?
Burksizm.value: Most of the time, those who grind or clench their teeth do not even notice it. The reason is that teeth grinding usually occurs at night during sleep. Therefore, it is quite easy to attribute or confuse the symptoms of teeth grinding with other problems. Bruxism is a little-researched medical term. So this term may sound foreign to you.

item1.title: What is Bruxism?
item1.value: Bruxism is the technical term for grinding or clenching teeth during sleep. Non-continuous bruxism is not a serious problem. Sometimes when we are very tired, dealing with something that occupies our mind, or annoying us, almost everyone may experience bruxism at some point in their lives. However, in cases of prolonged or continuous bruxism, it can cause various other problems. Many people, including us, may suffer from this problem and not even be aware of it. Frankly, the exact and definitive cause of bruxism has not been explained by the medical community. We cannot say that the medical community is very successful in finding an underlying cause. Recently, many new findings have emerged that contradict previous results. While researching teeth grinding, you may have come across a lot of information pointing to stress as the main cause. However, new evidence shows that stress alone is not the culprit. First of all, it is useful to examine bruxism under two different headings: night and day.

item2.title: Daytime Bruxism
item2.value: Although night grinding and daytime clenching seem similar, they are actually quite different situations. While teeth grinding is much more common in night bruxism, teeth clenching is more common for daytime patients. Although night grinding is much more common, daytime bruxism is reported more because it is easier to detect. There is no close relationship between the two: suffering from one does not mean you will be affected by the other. If you clench or grind your teeth during the day, you will probably notice it. This is not the case for nighttime occurrences. You may have been suffering from night bruxism for a long time without even realizing it. It is likely that you confuse the symptoms with other problems. Daytime bruxism has been associated with high-stress careers. It is very common in daily work stress and especially during exam periods in students.

item3.title: How to Understand If You Grind Your Teeth at Night?
item3.value: Symptoms of bruxism are not always obvious. First, your body tries to adapt to all adverse conditions. Therefore, it is easy to get used to the symptoms and not notice them. Second, some of the most common symptoms can be caused by other factors or confused with other symptoms.

item4.title: Symptoms of Bruxism
item4.value: Many people suffer from sleep bruxism and do not know it until complications develop. Understanding the symptoms is the first step in recognizing it. The list is more varied and longer than you might expect;
item4.item5: Cracks or fractures in dental prostheses

item5.title: Generally Accepted Causes of Bruxism
item5.value: Stress and anxiety disorder are the most common causes attributed to bruxism. However, over time, many causes have been considered, including malocclusion and infectious diseases. Recent studies have shown that genetic predisposition also plays a role. The only thing science is sure of is that bruxism is triggered by the nervous system. Bruxism has been associated with depression, work anxiety, and severe stress. It is even seen in children due to anxiety, not negligible at all. Teeth grinding and clenching may help some people keep their airways open at night. Blocked airways are the underlying cause of both night grinding and obstructive sleep apnea in some people.

item6.title: Dangers of Sleep Apnea
item6.value: Like bruxism, the severity of sleep apnea can vary. If you have sleep apnea and think it is mild, you should still be checked by a doctor. They will likely perform a sleep study to test for obstructive sleep apnea. The risks of ignoring sleep apnea are quite serious.

item7.title: How to Stop Night Teeth Grinding?
item7.value: Mild bruxism may not require treatment. It may disappear on its own when stress or anxiety is eliminated. However, if your teeth grinding is frequent and/or severe, you need to take precautions. Your teeth are in danger. Wear, cracks, and even fractures can occur slowly but irreversibly. The effects of teeth grinding and clenching do not appear suddenly; they accumulate over time. Furthermore, if your bruxism is related to OSA, there may be much more to it. Remember that lifestyle choices can contribute to the severity of bruxism. Smoking, caffeine, and alcohol are considered triggering and aggravating causes of bruxism. Reducing them can help reduce your bruxism. Dental splints are the longest-standing preventative measure for bruxism treatment.

item8.title: Dental Splints
item8.value: Some recent studies have shown that dental splints can worsen OSA while protecting your teeth. But it should be remembered that these mouth splints are definitely not a cure for bruxism. They are only to protect your teeth from the bad and destructive effects of bruxism. If your problem is night bruxism, it is recommended that you first go for a sleep apnea check-up and then have mouth splints made by your dentist. Perhaps this problem of yours will be resolved with sleep apnea treatment without the need for splints. If your problem is daytime bruxism, mouthguards really are your only option.

item9.title: CPAP Device
item9.value: CPAP stands for Continuous Positive Airway Pressure. A CPAP device is essentially a pump that pressurizes air after purifying it. If you have teeth grinding associated with OSA, this is exactly what you need. A CPAP machine is basically a small air pump. You place it on your face with a mask or nasal piece. This piece is connected to the machine by a hose. Continuous air circulation helps regulate breathing and combat airway obstruction. CPAP devices are the industry standard for treating sleep apnea. Your dentist can make a night guard for you to use with the machine. In some cases, this device alone may be enough to stop OSA and bruxism. Still, teeth grinding and OSA are difficult to detect on their own. This may not seem very serious to you. However, if you think you may be suffering from bruxism or OSA, it is very important to visit a dentist. If the problem persists, it can lead to bigger problems than your dental health.

DENTURE.title: What is a Denture?
DENTURE.title2: Which Type of Denture Is Right for You?
DENTURE.value: Dentures are artificial teeth, fixed or removable, intended to replace natural teeth. They can cover an entire jaw or just individual teeth. Dentures help patients with appearance, confidence, and comfort in speaking, eating, and smiling. Dentures typically last 5 to 10 years. Most require maintenance over time, such as adjustments or adding new teeth. Below you can find an informative guide prepared with our dental team. Compare types and materials and explore the pros and cons.

typeOfDenture.title: Types of Dentures
typeOfDenture.value: Depending on the condition of your mouth, you have several options to choose from. Not everyone is suitable for every type of denture. If you have no teeth; you will need a full denture. If you have some teeth; it depends on your dentist whether to extract the remaining teeth to make a partial denture (also known as a clasp denture).

item1.title: Complete Dentures
item1.value: Complete dentures contain 12 to 14 teeth per jaw. Some end at the first molar (6th tooth), but sometimes a second molar (7th tooth) is added for strength. Determining factors are the space available and the presence of opposing teeth. When choosing, there are two options

item1.title: First
item1.value: Conventional palatal dentures applied on the edentulous jaw. In conventional dentures, the upper arch covers the entire roof of the mouth and can be attached by suction. The lower denture is horseshoe-shaped and is a bit more difficult to use because of the moving tongue.

item2.title: Second
item2.value: Implant-retained dentures provide the most support and comfort. They also help reduce bone loss, meaning the oral condition will not continue to deteriorate. However, they still need to be removed and cleaned after every meal. At least 2 support implants are required for the lower jaw, and 2 to 4 support implants for the upper jaw. The implants have knobs on them. The denture has sockets for these inside the teeth.

item2.title: Partial Dentures
item2.value: If some teeth remain per arch, you may consider partial dentures. This solution can be supported by metal clips attached to adjacent teeth. Pink or gum-colored plastic can be added to the denture to make it more realistic. Resin usually covers a metal framework or implants.

item3.title: Flipper Teeth (Temporary Partial Dentures)
item3.value: Temporary dentures are another solution for those who do not want to be without teeth. They can be made before natural teeth are extracted or within 7 to 10 days after extraction. They allow you to visit your dentist less often. A temporary flipper tooth can be made for one or more teeth. They can be held with clasps similar to a retainer. When a winged tooth is placed in a space, it also prevents other teeth from shifting. It is very easy to remove and clean at night.

item4.title: What are dentures made of?
item4.value: Dentures have three main components: base, teeth, and framework.

item1.title: Base
item1.value: Denture bases are almost always made of acrylic resin or crown cobalt metal. The first is better for aesthetics because it is colored to match the patient's gums. The second is more durable and less likely to break if the denture is dropped. Flexible dentures are mostly made of thermoplastic materials. They are made for patients with excessive bone loss in the jaw. They are not as easy to use and get used to as others.

item2.title: Teeth
item2.value: Acrylic resin is the most popular material for fake teeth. It is light and inexpensive. The material also adheres easily to the base. There are also many color options. This is very important for partial dentures when the teeth need to match the pre-existing tooth structure. Porcelain teeth can also be made on the denture if desired. The appearance and feel of tooth enamel can be perfectly matched. This option is more durable than acrylic. Disadvantages include that porcelain is expensive and prone to breakage. When such a tooth is damaged, replacing it is much more expensive. Also, porcelain teeth are much heavier than acrylic ones, making them less comfortable to use. They are not often preferred by dentists.

item3.title: Framework
item3.value: Denture frameworks need a strong material to maintain shape. This is usually some type of metal such as nickel chromium, stainless steel, or gold. In partial dentures, the retaining clasps are mostly made of chromium cobalt. They combine strength and flexibility to last for many years.

item4.title: How are dentures made?
item4.value: It takes at least 3 months for most dentures to enter your mouth. The process involves several appointments. This is to ensure the best possible fit and durability. Impressions are taken to determine the shape of the denture. In cases where dentures are needed immediately, impressions are necessary before teeth are extracted. Laboratory technicians first cast dental stone into the mold and then make the denture. Patients visit the dentist several times during this stage to make adjustments. After that, your denture will be ready to use. If implants are involved, this process will be more complicated and take longer.
